MEMORANDUM
To: Crypto Task Force Meeting Log
From: Crypto Task Force Staff
Re: Meeting with Representatives of Jito Labs, Inc. and Multicoin Capital
Management, LLC
On February 5, 2025, Crypto Task Force Staff met with representatives from Jito Labs, Inc. and
Multicoin Capital Management, LLC.
The topic discussed was approaches to addressing issues related to regulation of crypto assets.
Jito Labs, Inc. and Multicoin Capital Management, LLC representatives provided the attached
document, which was discussed during the meeting.

To: Commissioner Hester Peirce, Chair - SEC Crypto Task Force
From: Rebecca Rettig, Chief Legal Officer - Jito Labs
Greg Xethalis, General Counsel - Multicoin Capital Management, LLC
Date: January 29, 2025
Re: February 5, 2025 Meeting Topics
_________________________________________________________________________________
This memorandum briefly describes the topics to be discussed at the February 5, 2025 meeting
between Jito Labs (represented by CEO Lucas Bruder and CLO Rebecca Rettig) and Multicoin
Capital Management, LLC (represented by Managing Partner Kyle Samani and GC Greg Xethalis)
(collectively, the “attendees”), on the one hand, and you and members of the staff of the U.S.
Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”), including the Crypto Task Force (the
“Staff”), on the other. This memorandum is not intended to be comprehensive, but provides a
high-level overview of the attendees’ objectives for the February 5 meeting.
The attendees expect to address two main topics during the meeting: (i) the ability to include staking
as a feature in exchange traded products (“ETPs”) and (ii) potential models for staking in certain
cryptoasset ETPs. As set forth more fully below, we believe first that including staking as a feature
in certain ETPs will benefit investors, more accurately reflect the benefits of native network assets
and permit issuers to support the security of the networks in which the assets operate; and second,
that there are at least two viable paths with respect to staking in ETPs: (a) to allow a certain portion
of the assets in the ETPs themselves to be staked via service providers who run validators while still
allowing timely redemptions, or (b) to include a liquid staking token (“LST”) reflecting the staked
version of the native asset (e.g., SOL (native asset of the Solana blockchain):JitoSOL (LST)) such
that it would amount to the entire set of native assets being staked.
We look forward to discussing these matters with you and the Staff, and welcome any comments or
questions in advance of or at the meeting.
I. Staking as a Feature in ETPs
As the Staff is aware, certain issuers originally included staking as a feature in their applications for
ETPs for Ethereum’s native token, ETH. At that time, the Commission requested that the issuers
remove the staking feature from their respective ETP applications. We understand the Staff may now
be amenable to revisiting staking in ETH and other cryptoasset ETPs, including in connection with
new applications filed for a SOL ETP.
A. Staking Reflects The True Nature of PoS Native Tokens
Staking refers to the process in which validators in a proof-of-stake (“PoS”) blockchain, like
Ethereum, or in a delegated proof-of-stake (“dPoS”) blockchain network, like Solana, “lock up” the
network’s native cryptocurrency (e.g., ETH, SOL) to participate in and demonstrate their alignment
with the network’s consensus mechanism. In most PoS networks, validators participate in the
consensus mechanism — i.e., confirming transactions that settle to the network — by putting up or
1

otherwise holding a certain amount of the staked asset. Typically, there are rewards for performing
properly or consequences for failing to do so, or both, depending on the network. Staking builds
network security by ensuring validators have a vested interest in the proper performance of the
network.
Rewards generally take the form of transaction fees and newly minted units of a network’s native
asset. PoS networks grant validators the right to generate additional native cryptocurrency as a
reward for properly validating transactions, as well as the right to receive transaction fees and tips
paid by network participants in connection with sending transactions. These rewards are shared
between validators and stakers for participating in securing the network. Reward amounts and
mechanisms may vary by network, but the way in which rewards are generated by the network and
then distributed is open, public and transparent.
Critically, staking is an essential part of any PoS/dPoS blockchain and is an inherent feature of any
native token of such a network.
B. Liquid Staking
In addition to staking directly by or with a validator, individuals may participate in staking for
PoS/dPOS networks through liquid staking protocols. Liquid staking is a mechanism by which users
stake assets with one or more validators through a smart contract protocol and receive a receipt token
— the LST — evidencing the native assets staked and the rewards earned via the liquid stake. For
example, in the Solana ecosystem, a user can stake SOL in the Jito stake pool — across one or more
validator nodes — and in return, receive JitoSOL as a representation of the stake and the rewards.
1
Liquid staking can be designed to decentralize stake across validators, which provides for greater
network security.
When held, LSTs are generally freely transferrable, meaning they can be productively used allowing
the holder the benefits of their assets and the network the benefit of the staking alignment. A user can
withdraw their native assets from the liquid staking pool — typically with a short lag time — upon
supplying the LST to the liquid staking protocol. Upon redemption of the LST, the user will receive
the correct number of natively staked assets (i.e., the amount originally supplied to the protocol) as
well as the pro rata portion of rewards the user earned through their portion of supplied (staked)
assets. While the LST is identifiable as a separate asset, it derives its value from the native asset on
which it is based because the LST is interchangeable for a fixed number of such native asset.
C. Solutions For Prior Questions Relating to The Staking Feature
We understand that three primary issues drove removal of staking as a feature in previous ETP
applications: (i) managing redemptions efficiently and, where possible, consistent with a T+1
settlement cycle, as time requirements may conflict with native “unbonding periods” in PoS
1
https://www.jito.network/docs/jitosol/liquid-staking-basics/.
2

blockchains;
2
(ii) managing tax implications of staking in the context of a grantor trust; and (iii)
determining whether staking as a service creates a securities transaction.
At the February 5 meeting, we will discuss potential solutions that will address these issues.
II. Paths Forward In Permitting Staking in Cryptoasset ETPs
Given the critical role of staking of blockchain networks, we believe staking would be a net benefit
to these ETPs products and the overall crypto industry. Allowing staking of native cryptocurrencies
would enhance the safety and security of the networks in which these assets operate, and would align
investors with the unique features of these assets. Restricting staking in cryptoasset ETPs harms
(i) investors, by crippling the productivity of the underlying asset and depriving investors of potential
returns, and (ii) network security, by preventing a significant portion of an asset’s circulating supply
from being staked.
There are at least two viable models for staking in ETPs.
First, issuers and authorized participants (“APs”) can contract with reputable companies, such as Jito
Labs, that host validators for certain blockchain networks and provide secure staking environments to
stake the native assets held by the ETP (the “Services Model”). In the Services Model, staking
service providers will stake native assets on behalf of the ETPs; issuers and APs will have to
determine whether and how redemptions can be effectuated within a T+1 cycle due to staked assets
becoming available only upon an unbonding period. This is possible by, among other things, only
permitting a portion of the native assets to be staked with a service provider. With the right ratio
(e.g., staking only 40% or 60% of the total assets), the assets can be reasonably assured of prompt
redemption on a T+1 timeline.
3
Any staking rewards would accrue to the value of the shares, or
could be designed in the ETP trust agreement to be sold and distributed pro-rata to investors.
4
With
respect to the question of whether the staking in this model is considered a securities transaction, we
4
In the traditional commodity-based trust shares ETP model, the units of the applicable commodity per share ratio
will decline as the sponsor’s fee and other recurring or extraordinary expenses of the trust are paid over time. In a
staked cryptoasset ETP, it is possible (and for ETH and SOL almost certain) that the revenue from even partial
staking will far exceed the expense ratio of the ETP. As such, a SOL ETP that starts at .1 SOL/share could, in the
future, equal 0.11 SOL/share instead of 0.09 SOL/share. This mimics the favorable investor experience in zero or
negative fee ETPs that utilize securities lending programs to fully offset expenses.
3
ETP trust agreements and disclosure documents provide mechanisms for and disclosure related to suspensions or
delays in the ETP creation and redemption process. In determining the appropriate staking ratio to define in the trust
agreement, the ETP sponsor must consider the structure of the particular blockchain’s unbonding period, the
anticipated net flows of the asset, and the likelihood that the ETP would be capable of satisfying redemptions in a
timely order. The trust document would require resetting the percentage of assets staked on a predefined basis such
that, when the most recent creation, redemption and related bonding or unbonding action is completed, the ETP will
hold assets at the target stake. This mechanism would mimic the mechanical nature of allocated and unallocated
custodial account functions such as those incorporated into precious metals ETPs.
2
“Unbonding period” refers to the mandatory waiting period enforced by the network to allow someone to withdraw
staked or delegated tokens from validators. During this mandatory waiting period, tokens remain locked and cannot
be used, held or sold by anyone other than the validator. The unbonding period ensures the security and stability of
the network by ensuring that validators have sufficient stake to keep them aligned with the consensus mechanism.
Unbonding periods vary by blockchain network.
3

believe that regardless of the Staff’s determination on that question, staking should be permissible
and also will be possible in an ETP structure.
Second, rather than directly staking assets from the asset investment as in the Services Model,
investors may receive the benefits of staking through ETPs that hold LSTs (the “LST Model”) —
either a dual-commodity model (i.e., including both the native asset and the LST relating to that
native asset) or, in certain circumstances, a single-commodity model (i.e., 100% LST). The LST
Model will allow for redemptions within the required time period because a dual-commodity ETP
will not be subject to unbonding periods; specifically, rather than staking the native assets to generate
rewards, the LSTs will perform that function, allowing assets and rewards to be redeemed. The LST
Model addresses the redemption timeline to comply with the relevant rule and eliminates the
question of how the Commission should analyze staking as a service. The LST Model also simplifies
the creation-redemption mechanism, accounting, and grantor trust issues for the ETP and could be
operated consistent with precious metals basket ETPs such as WITE and GLTR.
The solutions and implications set forth above are not exhaustive. We believe that the staking feature
and any novel challenges arising out of it can be addressed through various solutions that are within
the Commission’s purview.
* * *
We appreciate the opportunity to meet with the Commission on these topics, as well as your desire to
engage transparently on issues relating to cryptoassets.
We look forward to a productive dialogue with you and the Staff.
4

February 4, 2025
Proposed Priorities for the SEC Crypto Task Force
Below are suggested principles and priorities for the SEC Crypto Task Force to keep in mind as it
tackles issues that impact the digital asset industry. There are several avenues by which to carry
out these priorities, including no action letters, guidance, advisory opinions, and rulemaking. We
welcome follow-up discussions on which avenue is best depending on the priority. Please reach
out with any questions.
1. Establishing Regulatory Principles – Establish principles for the Commission to adhere to
when regulating distributed ledger technology (DLT) and digital assets (DAs), including:
○ Recognizing that DAs include a variety of asset types (e.g., fungible tokens,
non-fungible tokens, and stablecoins), all of which require their own
considerations depending on the context of their uses (e.g., financial vs.
non-financial use cases).

Interim Chair Caroline Pham, CFTC
From: Ian Weisberger, CEO Coinroutes & Co Founder
David Weisberger, Board Member - CoinRoutes
We are pleased to comment on several of the issues to be discussed at the upcoming Joint
SEC CFTC Roundtable on Regulatory Harmonization Efforts. While there are good reasons to
harmonize rules and coordinate efforts between the agencies in the oversight of interconnected
Futures and Equities markets, the need to regulate Digital Assets brings it to a new level. As
you are aware, there are crypto assets that are deemed to be commodities, there is a robust
swap/futures market on those assets and there will be assets deemed securities. As a result,
unlike traditional finance, there will be transactions between spot commodities and securities
that requires a new regulatory approach.
In addition, the crypto market structure has evolved without regulation, yet it functions extremely
well for institutional investors. Arguably, it has become an excellent laboratory for
understanding how markets would function in the absence of rules such as legislated tick sizes,
prohibitions on locked or crossed markets, trade through protection and fee caps.
At CoinRoutes, we have a unique perspective into the functioning of crypto spot and derivative
markets worldwide. Our firm, founded over 7 years ago, is a market leader in the provision of
algorithmic trading software having facilitated over $500 Billion in notional value traded, across
spot and derivative products. CoinRoutes processes multiple terabytes of market data every day
and connects to all the major US and international exchanges.
While many commenters will tell you the crypto markets are not “orderly” and are ripe for
manipulation, our data shows them to be very transparent with lower barriers to entry than either
futures or equity markets under Regulation NMS. In fact, our recent transaction cost analysis
(TCA) shows that institutional orders using our algorithms can be handled at much lower trading
costs than for similar sized orders in regulated markets. For example, in 2025, CoinRoutes
handled over $12 billion in unconstrained spot crypto comprising more than 3000 large
institutional orders with an aggregate total execution cost of under 5 basis points from the
aggregated “far” side of the market. This result, which compares quite favorably to NMS
institutional order slippage, was achieved, despite markets that are consistently crossed, without
any tick size constraints, or prudential regulators looking for market manipulation. In overseas
perpetual swap markets, CoinRoutes software executed over $65 billion across over 22,000
large, unconstrained, institutional orders at an average improvement of 1.7 basis points from the
“far” side of the market. Such performance would be impossible in the current US futures
markets where market makers have a virtual monopoly at trading inside of the spread.

As a result of this experience, we urge caution in considering “normalization” of regulation that
would result in higher crypto trading costs in the U.S. while helping overseas competitors. We
will go into more detail as we comment on three of the topics you plan to discuss in your
roundtable.
Promoting Fair and Orderly Markets
The bulk of our commentary is on this question, as CoinRoutes is in the business of helping our
clients execute at low cost, with low market impact in both spot and derivative markets.
Considering those markets best align with the SEC and CFTC respectively, we will discuss spot
in the context of securities regulation and the perpetual swap markets in the context of futures
regulation. In both sections we will start with a comparison of the market structures and then
share actual execution statistics for CoinRoutes clients.
Spot Market Market Structure, Compared to NMS Securities
There are three main differences between the crypto spot markets and equity markets under
Regulation NMS: zero intermarket regulation, no tick size regulation and no fee regulation.
The result of these differences is a market with no substantive queueing at price levels, many
more price level / market combinations and a requirement to consider fees in all routing
decisions, particularly as markets on a gross basis are almost always crossed.
1. Queuing - In the crypto market it is virtually unseen to have significant order size across
multiple orders at the same price at the same time. We have not calculated the
percentage of time recently, but it was less than 1/100th of 1 percent when we last
measured this and have no reason to believe it has changed as the tick sizes are so
small, relative to the price of the asset, that it is much cheaper to price improve than to
try and “race” orders to the exchange. The result is less emphasis on high frequency
trading based on speed and a more competitive market that has lower barriers to entry.
2. More Market Data - To illustrate this point, we used CoinRoutes book aggregation
service to determine how many individual price/exchange combinations were within 1%
of the midprice for Bitcoin, which, considering its volatility, is a reasonable proxy for what
trading algorithms might consider. On average, this number ranges between 500 to
1000 unique combinations per side of the order book. As a reference, standard equity
algorithms rarely look beyond 5 price levels in their decision making, so the difference is
substantial. From a regulatory perspective, this shows how the crypto markets have
much more order competition than equities, proving that Reg NMS is likely
counterproductive in its stated goal of increasing it.
3. Fees are unconstrained - To understand the magnitude of this, consider that the average
institutional fee for top clients in spot crypto is 2 basis points (0.02%). Considering the
tick size for Bitcoin, as the largest asset, is 1 cent ($.01), that means the lowest fees
charged, at todays price of $115,000, is $23, which is 2300 times the minimum tick. This
compares to equity markets where access fees are a fraction of the tick size and is why

markets always appear to be crossed, but when fees are taken into account are not. We
would suspect that market structure experts from the equity world would look at this
situation and declare it “messy” and hard to navigate. The results we have shown at
CoinRoutes, however, clearly disprove that assertion. As stated earlier, CoinRoutes
clients achieved excellent results as shown here:

It simply demonstrates, with modern technology, the market can adapt to a market structure
deemed chaotic and unruly. It also shows, there is potentially a real risk of liquidity fleeing the
U.S. if it becomes much cheaper to trade on markets that are not subject to over-regulation.
Perpetual Swap Market Structure, Compared to Listed Futures
The main difference between the CFTC regulated futures markets and the perpetual swap
markets overseas is direct client access. All the markets have tick sizes set by the exchanges
and all are single counterparty markets insofar as it is very hard to manage margin across
platforms. The perpetual swap exchanges, in general, do have smaller tick sizes, however and
by allowing clients to connect directly, have more order competition. To put this in perspective,
the average tick size for Bitcoin perpetual swaps is 10 cents, and that is, quite often the spread
observed in each market. At the same time the tick size for the CME Bitcoin future is 5 dollars
or 50 times higher, with observed spreads often much larger, albeit for much larger size.
Putting this tick size difference in perspective, here is a chart of CoinRoutes client performance
for institutional sized orders on perpetual swap exchanges:

Notice that the performance vs the Far side shows more outperformance than vs the Mid price,
which is due to the fact that the bid is always below the offer price on the individual exchange
used. That said, the 1.7 basis points of outperformance is particularly important to
contextualize as the average spread is much lower than for CME products. The larger
outperformance of 6.5 basis points vs the cost calculator is indicative of the liquidity on the
perpetual swap markets compared to spot, where the performance was roughly ten times
higher. This leads to the conclusion that the perpetual swap market structure is extremely
efficient and provides a valuable service to those firms looking for low cost hedging or
speculation.
As with spot, we looked at the distribution of this performance as well. In the swap market, the
average, unweighted, order showed a slippage of under 2 basis points and the standard
deviation of performance was roughly 25 basis points. This consistency is shown in the
following dot plot that shows more outliers with positive performance driving the weighted
outperformance:

Public Dissemination of Trade Data
While it may not always be as it is today, the crypto markets are more transparent than
traditional markets. Crypto exchanges publish their full order books and trade feeds for free,
while on-chain data provides much more insight into large movements than traditional SEC filing
data. In response to the lack of “official” consolidated data, many companies, including
CoinRoutes, have created their own consolidation, while a number of firms take the publicly
available data to do the same thing. If the SEC or CFTC contemplated the creation of a
consolidated tape, however, it is important to point out how important fees and disparate tick
sizes would complicate that endeavor. Due to those factors, different firms with different fee
tiers at various exchanges would see the same data differently. That would limit the utility of
such a feed for the average investor, while the existence of numerous free sources of data
make it unnecessary.
It is also worth noting that supporting Best Execution reporting (Rule 605) was a major use of
consolidated data in the equity markets. Due to the differences between the markets noted
earlier, a consolidated tape would not be as useful in crypto, particularly since it would not likely
be superior to any of the public sources of data. At the same time, firms such as CoinRoutes
produce our own best execution reporting and the public data available would allow the leading
firms in the space to do so broadly.
Monitoring of Underlying Markets
There is certainly scope for improved monitoring of crypto markets, particularly for manipulative
behaviors such as “momentum ignition” as well as surveillance of potential conflicts of interest.

Such monitoring could improve investor confidence in the market, which would improve liquidity
and smooth out some of the volatility.
The key, however, to momentum ignition surveillance would be to aggregate the data of both
derivative and spot exchanges together, which does not exist today in the equity markets. The
reason this could be important is that the derivative markets have more liquidity, but those
markets and their participants use the spot price on reference exchanges for determining risk.
Thus, if an unscrupulous participant builds up a sizeable position long spot and short perpetual
swaps, for example, it is possible for them to profit by dumping the spot first, particularly during
illiquid periods, and then buying back the perpetual swaps after a wave of liquidations was
triggered. This past weekend, there was a Sunday night / Monday morning liquidation cascade
in the crypto markets that might have been the result of such a trading strategy. According to
coinglass.com
, over $1.6 Billion in notional value was liquidated, although it is worth pointing out
over 75% of the liquidations were in less liquid assets than Bitcoin. Were there coordinated
surveillance between the largest perpetual swap exchanges and spot markets, intentional
selloffs would likely be uncovered and participants would be more confident in the integrity of
the markets.
Conclusion: While there are many structural issues to work out over the long run as more
assets become tokenized, it is important to let innovation continue in the crypto markets
themselves. As more data becomes available to the regulators, we believe that it will become
readily apparent to the participants in legacy financial markets that the current regulatory
environment is overly prescriptive. As a result, we would suggest caution on how to regulate
the digital asset markets in the U.S., by focussing on issues such as market integrity via
surveillance and promoting the concept of best execution.

PROVING WHAT DIDN’T HAPPEN
Redefining Compliance Through Cryptographic Proofs of Absence
AUTHOR: C. S. THOMAS, Epistria, LLC Charles@Epistria.com
DATE: 22 September 2025
Abstract
Current compliance infrastructures are built on procedural controls, attestations, and audit
logs. These mechanisms can show what happened, but they collapse when regulators, courts,
or the public demand proof of what did not happen. This paper introduces a theoretical
framework for evidentiary compliance, establishing a taxonomy of cryptographic proof
structures that extend assurance beyond activity into absence. Beginning with architectural
fairness (Bias-Blind Behavioral Pattern Recognition), the progression advances through
destruction receipts (Ephemeral Initialization Vectors), lifecycle receipts (Cryptographic State
Transition Proofs), and relational reachability proofs (Relational Merkle Trees, or Audit-
Verifiable Compliance Receipts). Together, these constructs reframe compliance from a
procedural function into an evidentiary discipline capable of withstanding adversarial and
legal scrutiny. The framework not only anticipates emerging regulatory mandates but also
demonstrates competitive, operational, and ethical advantages for early adopters. Evidentiary
compliance marks a paradigm shift: from trust in process to verifiable proof of both events
and non-events.
Note to Readers
This paper bridges cryptographic techniques and compliance theory to address a
foundational gap in regulatory infrastructure: the inability to prove what did not happen.
Readers from compliance and regulatory backgrounds will encounter cryptographic concepts
(Merkle trees, hash functions, initialization vectors) that may be unfamiliar but are explained
in context — technical expertise is not required to follow the core argument.
Readers from technical backgrounds will find familiar primitives applied in an unfamiliar way:
to compliance challenges that may appear procedural but carry profound legal, financial, and
operational consequences.
The progression from Section 3 onward traces how each technical innovation emerged from
a specific compliance limitation discovered in practice. Readers primarily interested in
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 1

practical applications may wish to focus on Sections 9–10 and Appendix A & F, while those
seeking technical depth should examine Section 7 and Appendix B.
The aim is not simply to describe new tools but to propose a theoretical framework for
evidentiary compliance — a foundation for future standards, regulation, and research.

1. Introduction: The Blind Spot in Compliance
Compliance has always been an exercise in documenting activity. Organizations generate
logs, attestations, and audit trails to show what was done. Yet when regulators or courts ask
the harder question — can you prove what did not happen? — the system falls silent. Logs can
confirm events, but they cannot establish the absence of events. Silence is taken as
assurance, and under pressure, silence collapses.
This recurring fragility can be described as evidentiary
debt: the accumulation of unanswerable questions
about non-events. Like technical debt or decision debt,
evidentiary debt builds silently within organizations
until it is exposed under stress. When regulators
demand proof of non-access, or when courts require
evidence that a prohibited transaction never occurred,
procedural systems default to absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence. The
result is collapse — whether in wrongful prosecutions, massive fines, or systemic loss of
trust.
What is missing is not more procedure but a shift in evidentiary design — from process-based
trust to cryptographic proof.
This paper proposes a theoretical framework for evidentiary compliance built on a
progression of cryptographic constructs. It begins with architectural fairness (Bias-Blind
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 2
Example of Evidentiary Debt
When Equifax was breached in 2017,
investigators could confirm which records were
accessed but could not prove which of the 147
million were untouched. The absence of
evidence was not evidence of absence. This gap
multiplied legal exposure and public distrust —
the very hallmarks of evidentiary debt.

Behavioral Pattern Recognition), which renders impermissible comparisons undefined by
design. It then introduces destruction proofs (Ephemeral Initialization Vectors) to ensure
irreversible deletion, extends those into lifecycle receipts (Cryptographic State Transition
Proofs) that span creation through destruction, and generalizes further into relational proofs
(Relational Merkle Trees or Audit-Verifiable Compliance Receipts) that establish both
reachability and non-reachability across systems.
Taken together, these layers form a taxonomy of compliance receipts that moves beyond
procedural assurance, offering cryptographic verification not only of events but of their
absence. In doing so, they provide the infrastructure needed to address evidentiary debt
before it accumulates into collapse.
Before developing this taxonomy in detail, it is necessary to acknowledge the tools
organizations already rely upon. Audit logs, blockchain-based ledgers, and zero-knowledge
proofs each address fragments of the compliance problem. They capture activity, secure
records against tampering, or protect sensitive disclosures. Yet none of them are designed to
establish evidentiary proof of absence. Each falls short when the compliance question shifts
from what happened to what demonstrably did not. Understanding these limitations is
essential, because they reveal why a new evidentiary framework is required and why
procedural controls alone cannot withstand regulatory or legal stress. To see why this debt
persists, we turn first to the tools most relied upon today — logs, blockchains, and zero-
knowledge proofs — and examine why none can fill the gap.
2. Existing Approaches and Why They Fall Short
Compliance infrastructures today rest on three main technological pillars: audit logs,
blockchain-based ledgers, and zero-knowledge proofs. Each has value, but each was
designed for a different purpose. When pressed to answer evidentiary questions about what
did not happen, all three collapse.
Audit Logs.
Audit logs are the default instrument of compliance. They record actions, capture user
identities, and timestamp events. They are indispensable for forensic reconstruction, yet by
their very nature they are silent on non-events. A log can show that an access occurred, but it
cannot show that no access occurred. Absence of an entry is not evidence of absence; it is
merely absence of evidence. Moreover, logs are mutable. Even when protected, they require
trust in the system operator to maintain integrity. In adversarial or legal settings, their
evidentiary value is fragile.
Blockchain-Based Compliance Systems.
Blockchains are often invoked as compliance tools because they provide immutability: once a
record is written, it cannot be altered without detection. But blockchains, too, only preserve
what is written. They cannot prove that an event never took place, only that a recorded event
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 3

has not been tampered with. Worse, their immutability can create an illusion of evidentiary
strength where none exists. An immutable ledger of incomplete records is still incomplete.
Blockchain does not address the compliance question most often asked in litigation: can you
prove that the alleged event did not occur?
Zero-Knowledge Proofs.
Zero-knowledge techniques demonstrate possession of knowledge without revealing it. They
are powerful in privacy-preserving authentication, and occasionally surface in compliance
discussions. But their orientation is different. ZKPs prove that a party knows a secret or that a
computation was performed correctly. They do not, however, prove that no prohibited path
was taken or that no unauthorized state was reached. They verify knowledge, not non-events.
Their elegance does not translate into evidentiary assurance for absence.
Why These Tools Are Insufficient.
While advanced cryptographic techniques, such as zero-knowledge proofs of non-
membership in a Merkle tree, can generate specific proofs of absence within a bounded set,
they are often designed to answer a single, predefined question. The framework proposed
here is fundamentally more holistic. It establishes a taxonomy of verifiable receipts that
prove absence across multiple dimensions: architectural capability (BB-BPRF), temporal state
(EIV/CSTP), and relational pathways (RMT/AVCR). This moves beyond point solutions to
provide a comprehensive evidential framework capable of addressing the systemic nature of
evidentiary debt.
The common flaw is structural. Each of these mechanisms provides assurance about what is
present — an entry in a log, a block in a chain, a secret known. None provide assurance about
what is absent. In regulatory or legal settings, this distinction is decisive. Organizations are
increasingly asked not only to demonstrate activity, but to prove inactivity: no trade, no
access, no bias variable. Current tools, however valuable in their domains, cannot bear that
burden.
If conventional tools cannot provide evidence of absence, the alternative is to begin with
architectures that render impermissible actions undefined by design. This is the role of Bias-
Blind Behavioral Pattern Recognition.
3. Bias-Blind Behavioral Pattern Recognition (BB-
BPRF)
The starting point for this framework was not data destruction or lifecycle receipts but
fairness. Bias-Blind Behavioral Pattern Recognition (BB-BPRF) was developed to address a
central flaw in machine learning systems: their reliance on between-group comparisons.
Conventional approaches attempt to mitigate bias through statistical adjustments or post-
processing of outputs. These methods treat fairness as a matter of calibration or correction.
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 4

BB-BPRF took a different path. It sought to eliminate the possibility of such comparisons at
the architectural level. By redefining variance structures, it made between-group variance
undefined rather than merely filtered or suppressed. In effect, the system itself could not
perform the comparisons that create discriminatory outcomes. This approach reframed
fairness not as a statistical afterthought but as a structural guarantee.
Yet the development of BB-BPRF surfaced a deeper problem. Architectural guarantees alone
are not self-enforcing. A system can claim that it prevents impermissible comparisons, but
without cryptographic evidence of how states were created, used, or destroyed, the guarantee
cannot withstand adversarial scrutiny. Regulators and courts require more than design intent;
they require proof. This realization led directly to the concept of Ephemeral Initialization
Vectors (EIV), in which fairness was no longer asserted as a procedural matter but enforced
and verifiable at the cryptographic layer.
4. Ephemeral Initialization Vectors (EIV)
The recognition that architectural guarantees must be paired with verifiable enforcement led
to the development of Ephemeral Initialization Vectors (EIV). In cryptographic practice,
initialization vectors seed encryption operations, shaping the security of stored or transmitted
data. Traditional designs treat these vectors as incidental — a technical parameter that can be
retained or discarded at will.
EIV reframes them as evidence. By design, EIVs are created for single use and then destroyed,
with destruction itself producing a cryptographic receipt. This receipt is verifiable by
independent parties, demonstrating not only that a particular key or vector was used, but that
it no longer exists. What results is proof of irreversibility: the assurance that sensitive material
has passed beyond recovery, regardless of institutional claims or procedural attestations.
The compliance significance is direct. Regulations such as the GDPR’s “right to be forgotten”
or HIPAA’s data retention rules require organizations to prove destruction of personal data.
Current practice relies on trust in process — a system operator asserts that deletion occurred.
EIV receipts replace this assertion with evidence. They transform destruction from a
procedural claim into an auditable event that is cryptographically verifiable.
Yet as with Bias-Blind, the solution revealed its own limit. Destruction proofs alone cannot
address the full scope of compliance. Data and systems undergo multiple transitions:
creation, use, modification, expiry, and destruction. Each state change is potentially subject to
regulatory or contractual scrutiny. EIV receipts solve for destruction, but compliance requires
receipts for the entire lifecycle. This gap pointed to the next step: Cryptographic State
Transition Proofs (CSTP).
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 5

5. Cryptographic State Transition Proofs (CSTP)
While EIV receipts provided verifiable evidence of destruction, they addressed only one point
in the lifecycle. Most compliance obligations extend far beyond deletion. Records must be
created according to specification, remain valid for prescribed periods, be updated in
controlled ways, and finally be destroyed. Each state carries its own regulatory and
contractual implications. Without evidence across the entire sequence, organizations cannot
demonstrate compliance with confidence.
Cryptographic State Transition Proofs (CSTP) generalize the logic of EIV to the full lifecycle of
an asset. Each state change — creation, validation, modification, expiration, destruction —
generates a receipt. These receipts are not independent fragments but chained together,
ensuring continuity of evidence across time. The system produces not only a record of what
occurred but a verifiable chain of state transitions, resistant to tampering and auditable by
independent parties.
The Transition State Model refines this concept by accommodating intermediate states.
Many compliance regimes do not operate in binaries of valid versus invalid, but through multi-
step processes — pending review, conditionally active, temporarily suspended. CSTP receipts
capture these nuances without losing the continuity of proof.
The Graph Lifecycle Model extends further. Modern organizations rarely handle assets in
isolation; records, systems, and workflows are interdependent. A single data object may feed
multiple processes, trigger downstream obligations, or exist simultaneously in multiple
contexts. Graph Lifecycle modeling applies CSTP receipts to these complex topologies,
enabling auditors to verify not just the history of an individual asset but the compliance
posture of entire networks of interdependent states.
CSTP thus moves compliance evidence from isolated events to comprehensive lifecycle
assurance. Yet even this is not sufficient. Compliance obligations often arise not from the
properties of individual assets or systems but from their relationships. A regulator may ask
not simply whether a record was destroyed, but whether it was ever accessible to an
unauthorized party. Lifecycle proofs cannot answer relational questions. Meeting that need
requires extending receipts into relational space, which leads to Relational Merkle Trees and
Audit-Verifiable Compliance Receipts.
Lifecycle receipts document events in sequence, but they cannot answer relational questions.
Regulators often ask not just what happened, but whether a prohibited path ever existed.
Relational Merkle Trees and Audit-Verifiable Compliance Receipts extend proofs into this
domain.
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 6

6. Relational Merkle Trees / Audit-Verifiable
Compliance Receipts (RMT / AVCRs)
Lifecycle proofs establish that an asset passed through creation, modification, and
destruction in a compliant sequence. Yet compliance questions often extend beyond the
history of a single record. Regulators, courts, and counterparties increasingly ask relational
questions: Was this asset ever accessible to that party? Did any unauthorized path exist
between this user and that data set? Lifecycle receipts cannot answer such queries because
they describe events, not relationships.
Relational Merkle Trees (RMT), and their generalized form as Audit-Verifiable Compliance
Receipts (AVCRs), extend cryptographic receipts into the relational domain. Instead of proving
that an event occurred, they prove the existence or non-existence of a pathway. By structuring
entities and their connections into a Merkle framework, the system can produce compact
proofs that a given relation does or does not exist. A bank could prove that no unauthorized
trade path was available; a hospital could prove that no patient record was reachable by an
uncredentialed user; an AI developer could prove that no protected class variable influenced a
decision.
The novelty is in the proof of non-reachability. Traditional systems can show that an access
occurred. RMT/AVCRs demonstrate that an access could not have occurred, because no valid
path existed. These proofs are cryptographically verifiable and auditable by independent
parties without requiring trust in the operator’s infrastructure.
This capability reframes compliance. Architectural guarantees require cryptographic
verification. Compliance proofs must span entire lifecycles, not just endpoints. Relational
systems demand relational proof structures. By addressing relationships as well as events,
AVCRs provide the missing evidentiary foundation. They enable organizations not merely to
assert, but to demonstrate, that prohibited interactions never took place.
Taxonomy at a Glance: Addressing Evidentiary Debt
Evidentiary debt arises when organizations cannot prove what did
not happen. The following receipt structures form a progression of
cryptographic tools designed to eliminate that debt:
BB-BPRF (Architectural Fairness): Removes impermissible
comparisons at design level.
EIV (Destruction Proofs): Receipts proving irreversible deletion of
sensitive material.
CSTP (Lifecycle Proofs): Chained receipts across creation,
modification, expiry, and destruction.
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 7

Graph Lifecycle (Systemic): Extends lifecycle receipts to
interdependent networks and workflows.
RMT / AVCR (Relational Proofs): Demonstrates reachability or non-
reachability — proof of what did not occur.
Unifying Principle: Evidentiary compliance converts procedural trust
into verifiable law.
7. Practical Considerations and Limits
Any theoretical framework must contend with practical realities. Audit-verifiable receipts add
computational and operational demands, and these must be acknowledged honestly.
Computational Overhead.
Receipt generation involves hashing, signature operations, and path construction within
Merkle or related structures. Verification requires path validation. In practice, these operations
scale logarithmically with the number of assets. For a system managing ten million records, a
proof path requires ~20 hash operations. Commodity CPUs routinely perform millions of
hashes per second, meaning verification completes in microseconds. Even at enterprise
scale, the bottleneck is not cryptographic cost but system integration.
Storage Requirements.
Storage is not the problem it once was. At roughly 512 bytes per receipt, even one billion
receipts per year (~500 GB) is easily accommodated by modern infrastructure. At cloud rates
of <$20/TB/month, even 100 TB/year is economically negligible compared to compliance
fines or litigation costs. The real challenge is not capacity but indexing and retrieval: ensuring
receipts remain queryable, portable, and verifiable across decades of retention and multiple
organizations. Designing scalable receipt registries, APIs, and archival standards is therefore
a more pressing issue than raw storage volume.
Implementation Challenges.
Integrating receipts into legacy systems is non-trivial. Existing compliance infrastructures are
narrative-based: they assemble logs and attestations into a story for auditors. Receipts
change the paradigm to proof-based compliance. Migration will require both technical
adaptation (receipt engines and verifiers embedded in workflows) and cultural change
(compliance teams trained to reason from proofs rather than logs).
Why Logs, Blockchains, and Zero-Knowledge Proofs Remain Insufficient.
Logs capture activity, blockchains secure immutability, and zero-knowledge proofs protect
secrecy. None provide proof of absence. This structural gap is why receipts are necessary
despite overhead.
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 8

Balancing Costs and Benefits.
The incremental costs — extra hashing, modest storage, new indexing schemes — are
predictable and bounded. The benefits are disproportionately large: streamlined audits,
reduced litigation exposure, faster regulatory response, and the ability to prove non-events
when it matters most.
In short, evidentiary compliance introduces friction, but it is predictable friction, offset by
outsized risk reduction. The shift from procedural trust to cryptographic proof is not just
feasible, it is overdue.
The practical challenges are real but bounded. And once the costs are understood, the
advantages extend well beyond compliance. Receipts create strategic opportunities as well
as safeguards
8. Toward a Theory of Evidentiary Compliance
The preceding sections describe a progression of constructs — from architectural fairness to
destruction receipts, from lifecycle proofs to relational reachability. Taken together, these
constructs outline more than a sequence of inventions; they form the basis of a theoretical
framework for evidentiary compliance.
A Taxonomy of Proofs.
The taxonomy may be summarized as follows:
• Architectural Fairness (BB-BPRF): design-level exclusion of impermissible
comparisons.
• Destruction Proofs (EIV): evidence that sensitive material has passed irreversibly out
of existence.
• Lifecycle Proofs (CSTP): receipts that document state changes across an asset’s
existence.
• Systemic Extensions (Graph Lifecycle): receipts generalized to interdependent
networks.
• Relational Proofs (RMT / AVCR): evidence of reachability or non-reachability across
entities.
Each category extends the evidentiary scope, moving from attributes of individual systems to
the relationships among them.
Conceptual Vocabulary.
This taxonomy introduces a set of terms essential for evidentiary compliance: receipt, state
transition, reachability, non-reachability, lifecycle, irreversibility. These terms are not merely
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 9

descriptive. They provide the conceptual grammar for reasoning about compliance as an
evidentiary discipline rather than a procedural one.
The Unifying Principle.
Across all categories lies a single principle: compliance without cryptographic evidence is
procedural trust; compliance with it is verifiable law. Procedural controls may be necessary, but
they cannot bear the full weight of litigation or regulation. Only cryptographic receipts —
spanning architecture, lifecycle, and relations — provide assurance that survives adversarial
and legal stress.
This theory reframes compliance as an evidentiary science. It shifts the foundation from
checklists and attestations to verifiable proofs of both events and non-events. Like double-
entry bookkeeping or public key cryptography before it, evidentiary compliance represents not
an incremental improvement but a paradigm shift in how organizations demonstrate integrity.
A vivid example of evidentiary compliance in practice is the apparent conflict between the
EU’s GDPR and the U.S. SEC’s Rule 17a-4. GDPR grants individuals the “right to be forgotten,”
requiring deletion of personal data on request. Rule 17a-4, by contrast, mandates long-term
retention of financial records, with deletion expressly prohibited. Conventional compliance
systems can only offer procedural statements — either that the record was deleted (satisfying
GDPR while violating SEC rules) or that it was retained (satisfying SEC requirements while
violating GDPR). Neither statement provides verifiable proof that both obligations were
simultaneously met.
Receipts make reconciliation possible. Lifecycle receipts can demonstrate that a record was
cryptographically deleted for the purposes of GDPR, while relational receipts can show that
the same record was preserved in retention storage yet rendered unreachable to unauthorized
processes under SEC mandates. Taken together, these proofs establish that the record was
both deleted in one regulatory sense and retained in another — with no contradiction.
Analogous evidentiary debts are emerging in other compliance frontiers — from proving the
absence of forced labor in global supply chains, to bias-blindness in AI training, to carbon
disclosure integrity (see Appendix B for extended sketches).
What once appeared to be an impossible double-bind becomes a defensible evidentiary
posture. Regulators on both sides receive cryptographic evidence aligned to their mandates,
and the compliance team is no longer forced to choose between mutually exclusive
procedural attestations. These benefits will not arrive all at once. Organizations will adopt
receipts incrementally, moving from narrow use cases to systemic assurance.
9. Strategic Benefits of Evidentiary Compliance
Much of compliance is framed as defensive: avoiding fines, meeting mandates, surviving
audits. Yet evidentiary compliance also creates competitive advantages that extend beyond
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 10

risk reduction. Receipts, once integrated, generate operational efficiencies, enable new
business models, and open collaborative pathways that procedural trust cannot support.
Operational Efficiencies
• Audit automation. Receipts eliminate manual log reconstruction. Instead of
assembling narratives, auditors validate receipts directly. Audit cycles shorten from
weeks to hours, reducing staff burden and cost.
• Incident containment. When a breach occurs, receipts show what did not happen as
clearly as what did. This narrows scope, shortens investigations, and limits regulatory
disclosure obligations.
• Predictable overhead. Hashing and storage costs are bounded and scale
logarithmically, replacing today’s unpredictable compliance firefighting with routine
verification.
New Business Models
• Compliance-as-a-Service. Cloud or managed service providers can operate receipt
engines and verifiers on behalf of clients, packaging compliance evidence as a
product.
• Proof-bundled offerings. Financial platforms, AI vendors, or healthcare systems could
differentiate by embedding evidentiary receipts directly into transactions or workflows
— selling not only services, but proof that those services meet regulatory and ethical
obligations.
• Insurance and risk markets. Insurers may price liability differently for organizations
that can produce cryptographic evidence of absence, creating financial incentives for
adoption.
Partnership and Ecosystem Benefits
• Interoperable trust. Organizations that exchange receipts can demonstrate compliance
across supply chains, joint ventures, or cross-border data flows without duplicating
audits.
• Regulatory positioning. Firms with evidentiary compliance infrastructure will shape,
not merely follow, emerging mandates. By presenting receipts as de-facto standards,
they influence rulemaking and reduce uncertainty.
• Reputation and trust. Demonstrable absence of violations becomes a market signal,
strengthening relationships with regulators, investors, and the public.
Strategic Takeaway
Evidentiary compliance is not only about avoiding collapse. It is a platform for efficiency,
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 11

innovation, and trust. Organizations that adopt early will not just comply more securely; they
will move faster, negotiate better, and shape markets in their favor.
These strategic advantages translate directly to the balance sheet. Organizations evaluating
evidentiary compliance face a straightforward calculation:

• Procedural controls: $X million/year
• Insurance premiums: $Y million/year
• Legal defense (average): $Z
million/year
• Major incident risk: Catastrophic

million/year

• Major incident risk: Contained
The math is unforgiving. Organizations already spending millions on procedural controls,
insurance, and legal defense can redirect a fraction of that spend toward receipt
infrastructure and reduce their total risk exposure. The question isn't whether to implement
evidentiary compliance, but whether to do so before or after the next headline-making
collapse.
A staged migration shows that evidentiary compliance is achievable. The remaining task is to
articulate the principles that make it portable across domains, and the research questions
that must guide its future.
10. Migration Path & Interoperability
Adopting evidentiary compliance does not require a single leap. Organizations can progress
incrementally, beginning with narrow proofs and expanding to relational receipts as systems
mature. A staged migration reduces risk, aligns with regulatory priorities, and creates early
wins.
Stage 1: Destruction Proofs (EIV).
• Focus: Prove irreversible deletion of sensitive data.
• Use Cases: GDPR “right to be forgotten,” HIPAA retention limits, contractual destruction
clauses.
• Benefit: Quick adoption, direct alignment with existing mandates, minimal integration
complexity.

Appendix A — Evidentiary Collapse in Practice
The fragility of procedural compliance is revealed most starkly in moments of crisis. Across
domains — law, finance, consumer protection, and data security — organizations have relied
on logs, attestations, and reconciliations to satisfy oversight. Yet when challenged to prove
that something did not occur, these systems collapse. The following four cases — the UK Post
Office Horizon scandal, the Equifax data breach, the Société Générale rogue trading episode,
and the Wells Fargo unauthorized accounts — illustrate how evidentiary debt accumulates
and eventually breaks institutions. Each shows how cryptographic receipts could have
transformed silence and suspicion into verifiable proof of absence.
UK Post Office Horizon Scandal (1999–2019)
The Horizon IT system, introduced across the UK Post Office network, generated phantom shortfalls in
branch accounts. Lacking any means to prove the absence of unauthorized activity, the Post Office
treated its system logs as authoritative. Those logs showed transactions but could not rule out that the
shortfalls were artifacts of system error. In court, the absence of proof was misread as proof of guilt.
The result was catastrophic. More than 700 sub-postmasters were wrongfully prosecuted, many
imprisoned or financially ruined, in what is now acknowledged as one of the largest miscarriages of
justice in British legal history. The system’s failure was not only technical but evidentiary: it could not
produce verifiable proof that the alleged discrepancies had not occurred.
Had audit-verifiable compliance receipts been available, the system could have produced cryptographic
evidence demonstrating that no unauthorized transaction paths existed. Instead of silence or procedural
attestation, courts would have received verifiable evidence of absence. The tragedy of Horizon was
therefore not merely one of flawed software but of evidentiary debt that compounded into human and
institutional collapse.
Equifax Data Breach (2017)
In 2017, hackers exploited a software vulnerability to access the personal information of roughly 147
million Americans. Investigators could confirm which records had been compromised, but they could
not establish with certainty which records had not. Conventional audit logs, designed to capture
activity, provided no way to prove non-access.
This evidentiary gap amplified the crisis. Regulators and courts had to assume that all records were
potentially exposed. The absence of proof became equivalent to proof of exposure, leading to over
$700 million in fines and settlements.
With lifecycle receipts, Equifax could have issued cryptographic evidence showing which records had
never been reached by unauthorized processes. Liability and remediation could have been narrowed,

Société Générale Rogue Trader (2008)

When the scheme unraveled, the bank was left with losses of several billion euros, reputational

Over the course of several years, Wells Fargo employees created millions of unauthorized accounts to
meet aggressive sales quotas. Activity logs showed accounts being opened, but there was no receipt-
level evidence tying those accounts to customer consent. The bank relied on process attestations — that
accounts followed proper procedures — yet those processes were easily manipulated.
The result was predictable collapse. Regulators uncovered the misconduct, levied billions in fines, and

With lifecycle and relational receipts, each new account could have been cryptographically bound to
explicit customer authorization. Unauthorized accounts would not have been defensible, because the

Across these cases, the failure is the same: systems designed to track activity cannot produce evidence
of absence. When collapse comes — whether wrongful convictions, breaches, rogue trades, or
fraudulent accounts — the underlying debt is evidentiary. Each case demonstrates how receipts,

Appendix C — Conceptual Implementation Guidance
Evidentiary compliance does not require new cryptographic primitives. It assembles existing
tools — hashing, signatures, and Merkle structures — into receipt frameworks tailored for
compliance use cases. The following sketches outline how such systems could be
implemented.
Receipt Structure (Conceptual)
A compliance receipt is a compact record containing:
• Object identifier: Hash of the asset or state.
• Transition type: Creation, modification, validation, destruction, relation.
• Timestamp: Cryptographically bound, anchored to trusted time sources.
• Proof path: Merkle path linking the receipt to a verifiable root.
• Signature: Organizational attestation of the receipt’s authenticity.
Together, these elements allow independent verifiers to confirm the event or non-event
without accessing the underlying data.
Verification Path
Verification proceeds in three steps:
1. Hash Validation: Confirm that the receipt’s object identifier matches the asserted asset
or state.
2. Merkle Path Validation: Recompute the proof path to the published root. Complexity
grows logarithmically with the number of receipts.
3. Signature Check: Validate the organization’s attestation using its public key.
The verifier thus confirms both the integrity of the receipt and its position in the broader
compliance structure.
Anchoring Options
Receipts require anchoring to prevent tampering. Options include:
• External Timestamp Services: Trusted third-party timestamp authorities.
• Blockchain Anchoring: Periodic publication of Merkle roots to public or permissioned
ledgers.
• Cross-System Anchoring: Reciprocal anchoring between organizations in a supply
chain.

Appendix D — Glossary of Terms
Evidentiary Debt
The accumulation of unresolved questions about what did not happen due to reliance on
procedural trust rather than cryptographic proof. Like technical debt or decision debt, it
compounds silently until exposed under regulatory or legal stress, leading to collapse in
audits, litigation, or public trust.
Evidentiary Compliance
A discipline that reframes compliance from a narrative of procedures into a science of
verifiable proofs. Evidentiary compliance directly addresses evidentiary debt by producing
cryptographic receipts — compact, verifiable records that demonstrate not only what
occurred, but also what demonstrably did not.
Receipt
The atomic unit of evidentiary compliance: a compact, verifiable record documenting a state
transition, destruction, or relational property. Receipts replace procedural attestations with
cryptographic evidence.
Ephemeral Initialization Vector (EIV)
A one-use-only cryptographic vector whose destruction generates a verifiable receipt,
providing proof of irreversibility (e.g., deletion of sensitive material).
Cryptographic State Transition Proof (CSTP)
A receipt structure documenting lifecycle events — creation, modification, validation, expiry,
destruction — chained together to demonstrate compliance across time.
Graph Lifecycle Model
An extension of CSTP receipts to interdependent assets and workflows, enabling proof of
compliance across networks rather than isolated objects.
Relational Merkle Tree (RMT)
A Merkle-based structure capable of producing compact proofs of reachability or non-
reachability between entities, enabling evidence of both events and non-events.
Audit-Verifiable Compliance Receipt (AVCR)
A generalized receipt that extends across lifecycle and relational proofs, designed to be
independently auditable and verifiable by external parties.
Compliance-as-a-Service (CaaS)
A business model in which organizations provide receipt generation and verification as a
managed service, bundling compliance evidence into product offerings.

Appendix F — Integration Realities and Technical
Debt
The cryptographic primitives underlying evidentiary compliance are well-established. The
challenge lies not in the mathematics but in grafting these proofs onto the messy reality of
enterprise systems. The following sections outline key implementation challenges - not as
insurmountable barriers, but as the predictable friction that accompanies any significant
infrastructure shift.
Key Management at Scale
Cryptographic signatures require key management, and key management at enterprise scale
is complex - though hardly unprecedented.
A mid-sized financial institution might generate 10 million receipts daily. Each needs a
signature, which raises immediate questions: What entity signs? The system? The
department? The individual processor? This isn't merely technical - it's about establishing
chains of authority that courts will recognize.
Organizations will likely adopt hierarchical signing schemes similar to their existing certificate
infrastructures. System-level keys handle bulk operations, department keys sign significant
state changes, and executive keys authorize critical assertions. Hardware Security Modules
(HSMs) protect these keys, though throughput limitations (typically 10,000
signatures/second) require distributed architectures.
Key rotation adds complexity. Financial regulations often mandate annual rotation, yet
receipts must remain verifiable for decades. This means maintaining secure archives of
historical keys - much like organizations already maintain archived encryption keys for
regulatory discovery. When banks merge, they inherit these key archives just as they inherit
legacy systems, maintaining them grudgingly but functionally.
The nightmare scenario - key compromise - has established playbooks. If a signing key is
exposed, receipts signed with that key enter a "presumed valid but under review" status,
similar to how payment card networks handle merchant breaches. Not ideal, but workable.
The State Transition Mapping Problem
Real business processes resist clean state modeling. A commercial loan application might
have 12 statuses in the origination system, 8 in credit assessment, and 23 in the servicing
platform. These don't map neatly to the "created modified validated destroyed"→ → →
lifecycle that CSTP assumes.
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 30

Organizations will solve this through selective receipting. Rather than capture every internal
state change, they'll receipt the transitions that matter for compliance: application received,
credit decision made, funds disbursed, loan closed. The internal complexity remains in
traditional logs while critical transitions get cryptographic proof.
Error states and edge cases require special handling. When a system crashes mid-transition,
organizations will likely generate "exception receipts" that document the anomaly without
breaking the chain. Think of these as cryptographic incident reports - they acknowledge
something went wrong while maintaining evidentiary continuity.
The gap between business events and system states (verbal agreements, offline decisions)
will be bridged through "attestation receipts" - human-initiated receipts that capture
significant events outside system workflows. Not perfect, but better than the current practice
of hoping someone wrote it down.
Organizational Adaptation Patterns
Every department initially resists receipt infrastructure, but resistance erodes under regulatory
pressure.
Legal teams worry about discovery implications - every receipt potentially becomes evidence.
But they worried the same about email retention, and adapted. They'll develop receipt
retention policies that balance compliance requirements with litigation risk, likely keeping
receipts for required periods then destroying them under documented legal holds.
Operations teams concerned about latency will find that 30 microseconds of receipt
generation is negligible compared to network variance. High-frequency trading systems
already handle similar overhead from regulatory reporting requirements. Customer-facing
systems will buffer receipt generation asynchronously, maintaining responsiveness while
ensuring compliance.
Compliance teams lose some narrative flexibility - receipts provide binary proof rather than
explanatory wiggle room. But they gain something more valuable: defensible positions. "We
have cryptographic proof" ends many regulatory inquiries that would otherwise consume
weeks of explanation.
IT departments facing integration costs will proceed incrementally. They'll start with new
systems (easier to build in than bolt on), then tackle critical legacy systems during planned
modernization. Less critical systems might never get receipt capability - they'll remain in the
procedural compliance world until retirement.
How This Actually Unfolds
The adoption pattern is predictable because we've seen it before with SOX, GDPR, and Basel
III. Here's the likely progression:
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 31

Year 1-2: Pioneer Phase A few forward-thinking organizations implement receipts for narrow,
high-risk use cases. Perhaps a bank implements destruction receipts for GDPR compliance,
or a healthcare system adds lifecycle receipts for clinical trials. These implementations are
expensive, custom, and imperfect. But they work well enough to prevent a major fine or win a
lawsuit.
Year 3-4: Standardization Industry bodies develop receipt standards - likely competing ones
initially. Cloud providers offer "receipt as a service" APIs. Enterprise software vendors add
receipt generation to their platforms (badly at first, but improving under customer pressure).
The first major enforcement action where receipts would have prevented disaster makes
headlines.
Year 5-7: Adoption Cascade Regulators begin "strongly encouraging" receipt use without
mandating it. Cyber insurance companies offer premium discounts for organizations with
receipt coverage. System integrators develop migration playbooks. The technology becomes
boring - a checkbox feature rather than competitive advantage.
Year 8-10: New Normal Fresh graduates learn receipt-based compliance in school. Legacy
systems without receipts require special exemptions. Regulators mandate receipts for critical
sectors. Organizations compete on receipt coverage percentages in their annual reports.
Throughout this progression, implementations remain imperfect. Coverage is partial - perhaps
60% of critical transitions in Year 5, growing to 85% by Year 10. Some receipts are lost to
system failures. Key management occasionally fails. Courts struggle with technical details.
But even imperfect cryptographic evidence beats perfect procedural attestation. An
organization with receipts for most critical transitions faces regulatory scrutiny with
confidence. One without them hopes their narrative holds up.
The transition won't be smooth, cheap, or complete. But it's as inevitable as double-entry
bookkeeping was for Renaissance merchants or SOX compliance was for public companies.
The organizations that move early will shape the standards, influence the regulations, and
avoid the panic implementations that follow the first major enforcement actions.
Evidentiary debt is real. The tools to address it exist. The only question is whether
organizations act before or after the next collapse makes headlines.
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 32

Crypto’s Evidentiary Debt Crisis
Problem Statement
Cryptocurrency markets face a unique evidentiary challenge. Investigations and enforcement actions
often fail not because misconduct cannot be observed, but because the absence of misconduct cannot be
proven. Regulators and exchanges alike are left with evidentiary debt—the unresolved burden of
proving negatives.
Key regulatory blind spots include:
♦ Demonstrating that no wash trading artificially inflated reported volumes.
♦ Establishing that no front-running occurred before major transactions.
♦ Confirming that no unauthorized wallet access compromised investor assets.
♦ Verifying that no off-book trades manipulated prices behind the scenes.
Current State of Practice
Today, crypto exchanges provide audit logs and transaction records that document what occurred.
These artifacts are inherently activity-focused; they cannot attest to what did not occur. As a result,
when challenged, neither regulators nor market participants can produce definitive evidence of absence.
This evidentiary gap undermines both enforcement and investor confidence.
Possible Solution: Cryptographic Receipts of Absence
Recent advances in compliance cryptography enable the generation of receipts that prove absence as
well as presence. These receipts can function as tamper-evident mathematical attestations that a
prohibited event did not take place within a defined scope and timeframe. In practice, they would allow
exchanges to produce verifiable proof that:
♦ No wash trades were executed.
♦ No front-running transactions were admitted to the ledger.
♦ No unauthorized wallet access took place.
♦ No hidden order book was maintained.
Alignment with SEC Task Force Priorities
This evidentiary capability directly supports the Task Force’s stated priorities:
♦ Clear regulatory lines — Cryptographic receipts provide bright-line separation between compliant
and non-compliant activity, moving beyond subjective policy interpretation.
♦ Tailored disclosure — Receipts of absence can be standardized as a disclosure framework, giving
investors assurance in domains where traditional reporting falls short.
♦ Investor protection — By supplying mathematical evidence that no manipulation occurred, receipts
strengthen confidence in market integrity and reduce litigation risk.
Case Example: Nevada Litigation
In a recent Nevada case, a trust alleged that $9 million in crypto trades never happened. Neither the
exchange nor the plaintiffs could prove presence or absence conclusively. This evidentiary stalemate
illustrates the systemic weakness: without cryptographic receipts of absence, disputes devolve into
unverifiable claims, eroding confidence in both markets and oversight.

Conclusion
The SEC’s Crypto Task Force has the opportunity to close a structural evidentiary gap in digital asset
regulation. By encouraging or requiring cryptographic proofs of absence as part of compliance and
disclosure frameworks, the Task Force can transform crypto oversight from a trust-based regime into a
verification-based one—reducing evidentiary debt, enhancing investor protection, and strengthening
the integrity of U.S. markets.

Subject: Recommendation on Governance for Private Blockchain Operations
Dear Commissioners,
I hope this letter finds you well. On behalf of Gridtek, I would like to respectfully offer a
recommendation regarding the governance and regulatory treatment of private blockchains operated
by companies.
1. Governance Framework
We recommend that private companies adopt governance structures overseen by their board
members or equivalent governing bodies. This approach provides accountability, effective
succession planning, and continuity of access to the underlying technology, helping ensure
operational stability over time.
2. Commitment to Innovation
Gridtek has a strong interest in establishing governance structures that foster both stability and
innovation. By creating clear, transparent frameworks, private blockchains can serve as reliable
platforms that support technological advancement, encourage responsible growth, and sustain long-
term innovation.
3. Purpose of Coins
Coins issued on private blockchains should be designed primarily for governance, operational
functions, and utility within the ecosystem. Their role is to facilitate functionality and decision-making,
not to serve as investment instruments.
4. Transparency
All transactions on these blockchains should remain publicly visible. Transparency allows
stakeholders to maintain trust in the system while reducing the need for burdensome oversight.
5. Regulatory Considerations
We recommend that coins designed for governance and utility within private company blockchains
not be treated as traditional securities when they are not sold to institutional investors or listed on
public exchanges. Recognizing this distinction would provide clarity, reduce unnecessary burdens,
and encourage companies to innovate responsibly.
Conclusion
A framework that acknowledges the unique nature of private company-operated blockchains would
support innovation, ensure stability through structured governance, and maintain public trust through
transparent operations.
We appreciate your consideration of these recommendations and your ongoing efforts to balance
regulatory integrity with the advancement of emerging technologies.
Respectfully,
